system:
You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

    1│

    3│## IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF OHIO EASTERN DIVISION
    4│
    5│DAVID E. CAMERON, et al.,
    6│

    8│

   16│
   17│HESS CORPORATION, et al.,
   18│
   19│## **REPLY MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN RESPONSE TO PLAINTIFFS’ OPPOSITION TO MOTION OF MASON DIXON ENERGY FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT**
   20│
   21│Defendants.
   22│
   23│## **I. INTRODUCTION**
   24│
   25│In opposing Mason Dixon Energy’s motion for summary judgment, Plaintiffs make two arguments: First, they contend that Mason Dixon Energy’s assignments of their leases contained warranties of title and thus, the assignee (now co-defendant Hess Corporation) has grounds to cross-claim against Mason Dixon Energy seeking defense and indemnification of the challenges to title made by Plaintiffs in this litigation, precluding summary judgment for Mason Dixon Energy; second, they contend that Mason Dixon Energy was unjustly enriched when it ‘flipped’ the Plaintiffs’ leases to Marquette Exploration, LLC. Both of these arguments fail, as explained in this memorandum and as supported by the attached Affidavit of Asa Bowers of Mason Dixon Energy.
   26│
   27│In addition to these arguments, Plaintiffs included in their memorandum several pages of completely irrelevant and improper deposition testimony and unsupported commentary solely and unabashedly to “respectfully request this Honorable Court understand that Mason Dixon
   28│
   29│is, in fact, the primary bad actor in this action.” *Plaintiffs’ Response in Opposition to Defendant, Mason Dixon Inc.’s Motion for Summary Judgment* (ECF # 53) at 8. This gratuitous information is not ‘responsive’ to anything set forth in the pending motion and should not even be given any consideration in this context.
   30│
   31│## II. DISCUSSION OF LAW
   32│
   33│### **A. Plaintiffs failed to provide any evidence to dispute the material facts presented by Mason Dixon Energy, which facts show it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law**
   34│
   35│Rule 56 provides that “[t]he court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Rule 56(a), *Federal Rules of Civil Procedure*. Supporting material facts may be shown in a variety of ways as set forth in Rule 56(c), including an affidavit which sets forth facts which would be admissible in evidence. That is exactly what Mason Dixon Energy did in supporting its motion.
   36│
   37│In opposing a motion for summary judgment, it is not enough for the nonmovant to rely on speculation, allegations or supposition. “... ‘[R]ather, its response must ... set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial. If the opposing party does not so respond, summary judgment should, if appropriate, be entered against this party.’ Fed.R.Civ.P. 56(e)(2) (July 2010) (amended Dec. 2010).” *Newell Rubbermaid, Inc. v. The Raymond Corp.*, 676 F.3d 521 (6th Cir. 2012).
   38│
   39│Mason Dixon Energy properly supported its motion for summary judgment and explained why, as a matter of law, it is entitled to judgment. The primary material factual basis for the motion, as supported by the affidavit of Asa Bowers, is Mason Dixon Energy’s unequivocal assignment of the subject leases to Marquette Exploration, LLC, in December 2008. Not only do
   40│
   41│Plaintiffs not dispute the material facts as outlined in the affidavit, they concede them (“Plaintiffs do not dispute that Mason Dixon assigned the Leases to Marquette Exploration, LLC, or that Defendant, Hess Corporation, subsequently purchased the assets of Marquette Exploration, LLC, which included leasehold interests contained in the Leases.” *Plaintiffs’ Response in Opposition to Defendant, Mason Dixon Inc.’s Motion for Summary Judgment* (ECF # 53) at 4).
   42│
   43│Rather than to dispute some aspect of the affidavit with counter-evidence or to show the presence of other disputed material facts which might preclude judgment as a matter of law in favor of Mason Dixon Energy, in the manner authorized by Rule 56(c)(1), Plaintiffs instead ask the Court to surmise that the motion should be denied based solely on conjecture and speculation. Such an approach is improper, insufficient and should not be given any credence by this Court.
   44│
   45│### **B. Neither Hess nor Marquette has asserted any breach of warranty of title claims against Mason Dixon Energy**
   46│
   47│In *Plaintiffs’ Response in Opposition to Defendant, Mason Dixon Inc.’s Motion for Summary Judgment* at 4, Plaintiffs argue that Mason Dixon Energy is not entitled to dismissal by way of summary judgment on the declaratory judgment counts because Mason Dixon Energy warranted title to the Cameron and Griffith leases when it assigned them to Marquette Exploration, and “given the terms of the warranty, Mason Dixon is a proper party to all of the declaratory judgment counts (Counts I, II, IV, V , VI and VII) UNLESS Hess Corporation, and/or all other defendants, expressly and unambiguously declare that they are releasing Mason Dixon from its warranty obligation(s) under the assignment to defend against
   48│
   49│Plaintiffs' claims." *Id.* This argument is theoretical and meaningless in the context of the true posture of this litigation and in considering the claims which HAVE been asserted.
   50│
   51│Plaintiffs have it backwards, sideways and just plain wrong. IF the Hess defendants HAD asserted a cross-claim for breach of warranty of title against Mason Dixon Energy, then this litigation would be in a different posture than it presently stands, and who knows whether the pending motion would have been filed. But Hess has not made a cross-claim against Mason Dixon Energy for breach of warranty of title, so Plaintiffs' argument is moot.
   52│
   53│### **C. Mason Dixon Energy did not profit from assigning the Cameron and Griffith leases to Marquette**
   54│
   55│Plaintiffs' second argument, which is based upon pure conjecture, asserts that Mason Dixon Energy is not entitled to summary judgment on the unjust enrichment count because "Mason Dixon was unjustly enriched when it 'flipped' both Leases to Marquette Exploration, LLC for several thousands of dollars per net mineral acre after it acquired the Leases by paying Plaintiffs \$100.00 or less per net mineral acre. The enormous resulting profit for Mason Dixon upon flipping the Leases, which resulted from its unequal knowledge, was unconscionable." *Plaintiffs' Response in Opposition to Defendant, Mason Dixon Inc.'s Motion for Summary Judgment* at 7.
   56│
   57│Plaintiffs have provided no evidentiary support for the foregoing statement: that is because the statement is not true. Moreover, not only do the Plaintiffs simply pull that statement out of thin air, but then they compound the inaccuracy by urging the Court to
   58│
   59│understand that Mason Dixon is, in fact, the primary bad actor in this action. Though the remaining defendants are vigorously contesting the Plaintiffs' legal positions relative to the Leases, Hess Corporation at its related entities are third-
   60│
   61│party purchasers now forced to defend against these (and multiple other) claims cause by the deceptive business practices of Mason Dixon. Mason Dixon concealed material information relative to the value of the oil and gas rights it was seeking to acquire from Plaintiffs, and thereafter, agents of Mason Dixon intentionally and wantonly did whatever was necessary to get Plaintiffs', and multiple others, to sign their oil and gas rights away for an incredibly small fraction of the true value.
   62│
   63│*Id.* at 8-9. All of this is pure speculation, as shown by the attached Affidavit of Asa Bowers of Mason Dixon Energy LLC (this affidavit is authorized by and submitted under the authority of Civ. R. 7.2(d) of the Local Rules of Civil Procedure for the U.S. District Court for the S.D. of Ohio.)
   64│
   65│As shown by the affidavit, Mason Dixon Energy is a land services company. It does not invest and speculate in mineral rights; it does, however, provide land services to those who do. For this project, Mason Dixon Energy was retained by Marquette Exploration, LLC to research, negotiate and obtain leases for oil and gas rights in Jefferson County, Ohio. Mason Dixon Energy did so as the agent for an undisclosed principal: Marquette Exploration, LLC. Mason Dixon Energy's agreement and terms with Marquette included taking the leases in Mason Dixon Energy's name then later assigning them to Marquette Exploration. Mason Dixon Energy did not 'flip' the Griffith or Cameron Leases, nor any other of the Jefferson County leases, to Marquette, as Plaintiffs inaccurately state in their memorandum. The overall services provided to Marquette Exploration by Mason Dixon Energy included the lease assignments. This is a standard practice and protocol in the industry, when an exploration or production company seeks to retain anonymity.
   66│
   67│## **III. CONCLUSION**
   68│
   69│Based upon the foregoing, as well as its initial memorandum of law, the Defendant,
   70│
   71│Mason Dixon Energy, Inc., respectfully requests this Court enter an Order awarding it summary judgment on all counts in Plaintiffs' Complaint. Mason Dixon Energy has shown by affirmative evidentiary affidavits of one of its officers that it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law as against all counts in the Complaint. Plaintiffs' speculative arguments and mud-slinging have done nothing to dispute the material facts supporting that relief.
   72│
   73│Dated this 1st day of April, 2013.

Asa Bowers CEO Mason Dixon Energy LLC The foregoing instrument was acknowledged before me this 1st day of October, 2012, by Asa Bowers. Notary Public My commission expires April 12, 2022

Answer three things about the file above.

1. Does it contain an instrument, as defined? If not, return an empty
   `instrument_name` and say in `note` what the document is instead. If it does,
   name it and give the first and last line of the instrument itself — cutting
   off any filing that wraps it and any unrelated exhibit that follows.

2. Is this file one part of a document split across several files? The other
   files in the same bundle are listed above with their opening and closing
   words. If the instrument in this file begins part-way through a document
   whose earlier part is one of those files, give that file's name in
   `continues_from`; otherwise return an empty string. If this file's text
   breaks off mid-document rather than ending properly, set `ends_mid_document`
   to true.

3. List every substantive provision of the instrument, in document order. For
   each: a short name including its number if it has one; the first and last
   line it occupies; its text, repaired as described; and one sentence in
   `repairs` saying what you fixed, or an empty string if nothing needed fixing.

A line may hold more than one provision — the OCR often runs lettered
sub-provisions together on a single line. When that happens, give each
sub-provision the same line range and let the text tell them apart.
